# Fifth Pass — What Seventy Years Buys

*Same house style. The two questions from the hybrid brief are still open; I've stopped raising them. I'd only note that this brief arrives with the same architecture — a portfolio and pricing decision dressed as a creative one — and I'll design for silence again.*

---

## The thing that is not being said

Two decisions sit under this and neither is on the agenda.

The first is whether the under-35 decline is a **cohort** problem or a **life-stage** one. "Purchase share falling among under-35s" is a sentence that can describe two entirely different companies. In one, people have always entered this category at forty and always will, our current forty-year-olds bought nothing from us at twenty-eight either, and the decline is a rounding artefact of a fatter cohort ahead of a thinner one. In the other, a generation has genuinely walked past us and will not come back, and each year of delay compounds. Same data, opposite urgency, opposite budget. I'd want the cohort curves — penetration by birth year at equivalent age — before anyone commissions a font. That analysis takes a fortnight and it exists in our own panel data. Nobody has run it, which is itself informative.

The second is who pays. A rebuild of this kind is financed by the loyal base for three to five years and does not repay inside a single incumbent's tenure. If the objective is actually the next two annual plans, there is a correct answer and it is a harvest strategy executed honestly. That's a legitimate choice. It is not the choice we'd be making if we run this brief, and the two should not be confused in the same room.

## Why the last attempts were mocked, precisely

Not because they were modern. Because they were **claims**.

The previous campaigns changed the signals and left the substance alone: new voice, new casting, borrowed vernacular, the same product in the same pack at the same price on the same shelf. Under-35 consumers are not hostile to old brands. They are extremely good at detecting the gap between what a brand says about itself and what it costs the brand to say it. Modernisation announced through advertising is the cheapest possible signal, and cheap signals are read as fraud almost automatically.

And the loyal base didn't defect because we spoke to young people. They flinched because they were told, in public, that the thing they've bought for thirty years was embarrassing. That's the actual mechanism. It is entirely avoidable and it has nothing to do with tone.

So the operating principle for everything below:

**Change the substance, don't announce the change. Let relevance be discovered rather than asserted.**

If we run a campaign titled anything resembling *"We're Back"*, we will have repeated the exercise with a larger budget.

## The positioning

I would not reposition the brand. I'd reposition the **relationship**, and leave the brand where it is.

Heritage is currently being used as sentiment — *we've been here since 1955, wasn't that lovely*. Sentiment is exactly what a 27-year-old has no use for, and it is also what makes older customers feel curated rather than served. The same seventy years, used differently, is the strongest asset in the building: heritage as **evidence**. Not *we are old*, but *we have been doing one thing for seventy years and nobody alive does it better*. Longevity as proof of competence, not as a period costume.

That reframe does something structurally useful. It is not age-segmented. A 68-year-old and a 26-year-old can both find it credible, for different reasons, without either being told the other exists. Every campaign that fails here fails because it makes the two audiences visible to each other.

The tell that we've got it right: the positioning should be *demonstrable by the product*, and it should embarrass us slightly with how unfashionable it is. Craft, specificity, obsession, refusal to cut a corner nobody would notice. Those read as authentic because they are expensive, and they are expensive because they are real.

## Preserve versus retire

The internal argument — "how much change can the brand absorb" — is unanswerable as stated and trivially answerable as measurement. I'd stop debating it and instrument it. Two questions per element, asked of buyers and non-buyers:

**Do they recognise it? Do they attribute it to us?**

Anything scoring high on both is a distinctive asset and is not ours to retire regardless of how it looks in a deck. That includes the things the marketing team is most tired of — colour, shape, mark, jingle, the pack cue that lets a loyal shopper find us at two metres in bad light. Fatigue is an internal condition, not a consumer one. Assets take decades to build and an afternoon to destroy; the asymmetry is total.

Anything scoring low on both is a convention, not an asset, and can go tomorrow at no cost. Most of what we'd call "the brand" lives here: the typography, the layout grid, the stock photography, the descriptive copy nobody has ever read, the categories we sponsor out of habit.

What I'd retire without hesitation, because none of it is recognised or attributed: our **behaviours**. Where we advertise, who we cast, the occasions we claim, the price-pack architecture inherited from a retail environment that no longer exists, the assumption that the category is bought the way it was bought in 1998, and the tone of voice that talks about the consumer's family rather than to the consumer.

Retire conventions, preserve assets, change behaviours. That formulation ends the internal argument, and it ends it with evidence rather than seniority, which is why I'd expect resistance to it.

## Relevance is earned in product, not in comms

The single highest-leverage move: young consumers should encounter us in a **format, occasion or channel that didn't previously exist**, rather than encountering an advertisement telling them the old thing is now for them.

New pack sizes for smaller households. Price points that work for a first-time buyer rather than a stock-up. Formats built for occasions the founding generation didn't have. Availability where the under-35 shop actually happens — convenience, food service, marketplace, third-party curation, the places our excellent legacy distribution doesn't reach because it was built around a weekly big shop.

This is where the strong distribution stops being an asset and starts being a trap: it makes us feel present while being structurally absent from the moments in question. High awareness with low consideration is not a communications problem. It's a *shelf we're not on*.

And it protects the base perfectly. Nothing they buy changes. Same SKU, same shelf, same price, same taste. Recruitment happens adjacent to them, not on top of them.

## Channel and content

Three rules, and the third is the one that will be broken.

**Show the work, not the brand.** Process, makers, materials, the eighty-year-old machine, the person who has done this for thirty-one years. This travels natively in short-form video, it is genuinely interesting, it cannot be faked by a competitor, and it makes the identical point to both audiences without addressing either. Heritage brands have the best raw content in any category and almost universally decline to use it.

**Borrow credibility, don't buy reach.** Creators who already buy us, found rather than cast, given the product and no script. Small, specific, unglamorous, in numbers. A large paid celebrity is the same cheap signal that failed twice already, at higher cost.

**Do not perform youth.** No vernacular we didn't earn, no meme literacy, no self-aware "how do you do, fellow kids" reflexivity, which is now itself the most dated register available. The brand should sound like a seventy-year-old institution that is very good at one thing and slightly uninterested in your approval. Confidence reads young. Trying does not.

## Sequencing

The backlash requires an announcement. So there isn't one.

**Quarters 1–2: unannounced.** Cohort analysis, asset audit. Launch the new formats in limited geography or a single channel, with no master-brand campaign whatsoever. Content programme begins quietly and continuously, because it needs time to look like it was always there rather than like a launch. The base sees nothing at all.

**Quarters 3–4: evidence.** Read penetration, not sentiment. Keep what worked, kill the rest silently, and expand distribution rather than spend. Still no campaign. The absence of a campaign is doing real strategic work in this phase and will be the hardest thing to defend internally.

**Year 2: the pack, and only what the audit permits.** Assets survive intact; conventions get modernised. This is the only irreversible move in the sequence and it happens after the evidence, never before. Loyal shoppers should be able to find it without looking.

**Year 2–3: the master brand speaks**, once there is something true to say, and it says it as continuity — the same seventy-year claim, now with proof attached.

Reversible things fast, irreversible things slowly. We'll be wrong about several of these and I'd like to be wrong in the cheap ones.

## How we'd know

Penetration among under-35s, quarterly, and specifically the *second* purchase — trial is buyable, repeat is not. Cohort penetration curves against the same age band five years prior. Source of volume: new households versus our own existing buyers trading sideways, which is the failure that looks like success for four quarters. Base retention by SKU and by age band, watched weekly through any pack change. Attributed recognition of the assets we kept, before and after. Distribution in the new channels, which is the leading indicator for all of it.

One number I'd refuse to set: a social engagement or sentiment target. Name it and it will be met, by exactly the kind of content that caused the mockery the first two times.

---

## What I'd resist

The rebrand as opening move. The logo. A purpose platform. A celebrity. Any campaign whose subject is the brand's own transformation. Focus groups of nineteen-year-olds asked what they think of us, which reliably produces the advertising that gets mocked. Removing a distinctive asset because the team has seen it too often. Cannibalising the base's SKU to fund the new one. And the executive who has already commissioned the redesign and would like a strategy to arrive at it independently.

---

The pattern, once: this is a distribution decision, a price-pack decision, and a decision about who the next twenty years belong to — with advertising arriving afterwards to ratify choices we'll have already made elsewhere.

Which leaves the two I'd want and don't have: whether we are financing a rebuild or dressing a harvest, and whether the cohort curves have already been run somewhere I can't see. The second would make most of the above either obvious or unnecessary.

I'll assume, as before, that silence is an answer of a kind.
